newsitem.title: USA: BOJ, BUBA said unlikely to intervene in FX market.
newsitem.headline: BOJ, BUBA said unlikely to intervene in FX market.

text.p: Japan and Germany have entered into a verbal tug-of-war over the dollar exchange rate, but it will not lead to central bank intervention if the dollar adheres to current trading levels, U.S. analysts and traders said.

A slew of recent remarks from key finance officials, first from Japan and then from Germany, were successful at reining in the dollar from its recent 42-month high of 114.92 against the yen and a dip below 1.50 marks, experts said.
However, a dollar rise to between 115 and 120 yen or a drop to less than 1.40 marks could spur monetary authorities to trade currency reserves in an effort to manipulate exchange rates, experts said.
"What we are seeing right now is verbal intervention -- that's always the first step," said Bob Houck, vice president and trader at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.

"This market is so starved for volatility and a confirmation of which way it is going to go that verbal intervention will be enough and I don't envision intervention until around 1.40 dollar/mark and 120 dollar/yen," he said.
He said there was no threat of reaching these levels at the moment.

Lars Pederson, international economist at CS First Boston Corp, concurred, saying recent comments out of Japan were an effort to set the stage for Bank of Japan intervention if the dollar should rise to between 115 and 120 yen.

Also, Michael Faust, global portfolio manager at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser said that, given an obvious discomfort in Europe to dollar/mark trading below 1.50, a sharp sell-off lasting more than one session and dipping below 1.40 marks could "spark a little bit of intervention."
The dollar opened on Wednesday in the United States at 1.5052/62 marks and 111.40/45 yen.
Over a year has passed since central banks last intervened in the currency market, the longest dry spell since 1990, Faust said.

The last central bank operation was on August 15, 1995 when the Fed, Japanese monetary authorities and the Bundesbank coordinated to purchase in total $300 million against the yen and $400 million against the mark, according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
The dollar was trading near 95.02 yen and 1.4476 marks before the start of the operation, the New York Fed said.
U.S. officials so far have elected to stay silent regarding domestic dollar policy.

While market players have drawn various conclusions from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's silence, the dollar fell then rose in reaction to foreign officials' remarks. Almost all expect no imminent change to his long-standing strong-dollar policy.

"It's going to be a while before the official U.S. position changes as there are new faces in the Treasury and it will take time for them to get established," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
Faust does not anticipate any clear indication from U.S. dollar policymakers anytime soon.
"Right now, everyone else is talking for them and for better or for worse, they don't really need to come in and complicate the issue," he said.
The first hit to G3 strong-dollar policy came on Thursday from Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of Japan's Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau.
He said the yen depreciation since dollar/yen hit a post World War II low of 79.75 in April 1995 had peaked, sending dollar/yen from just below its recent high to a one-month low.

The dollar softness, combined with fresh signs of German economic weakness last week, dragged dollar/mark lower for four consecutive sessions. It eventually dipped below 1.50 marks, sparking comments from a host of Bundesbank members on Tuesday.

Dollar/mark started to recover after Bundesbank council member Edgar Meister said the dollar/mark rate was not appropriate, echoing earlier comments from fellow council member Hans-Juergen Krupp that a firmer dollar might seem more appropriate.
But it was Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's blatant support for the dollar that caused short-sellers of dollar/mark to buy in mass, reversing the downtrend.
But analysts warned that hot-air alone may not be enough to prop up the dollar against the mark, or the yen against the dollar long-term.

"The market may turn a bit more cynical and if all (Germany) is prepared to do is jawbone the dollar higher and not do anything else, then I think the market may view that as a selling opportunity," Faust said.
